etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English asken (also esken, aschen, eschen, etc.), from Old English āscian, from Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eys- (“to wish; request”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian aaskje (“to ask, demand, require”), West Frisian easkje (“to ask, demand, require”), Dutch eisen (“to demand, require”), German heischen (“to ask, request, implore”), Russian иска́ть (iskátʹ), Sanskrit इच्छति (iccháti) (whence Hindi ईछना (īchnā).

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To request (information, or an answer to a question).
(transitive or ditransitive) To request or enquire of (a person).
(transitive usually with 'for' or intransitive) To request (an item or service); see also ask for.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 7:7:
quote.text: Ask, and it shall be given you.

definitions.definition: To put forward (a question) to be answered.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, John 9:21:
quote.text: He is of age; ask him: he shall speak for himself.

definitions.definition: To require, demand, claim, or expect, whether by way of remuneration or return, or as a matter of necessity.

quote.citation: 1705, J[oseph] Addison, Remarks on Several Parts of Italy, &c. in the Years 1701, 1702, 1703, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: But in any Exigence of State, like that they are now pressed with, it certainly asks a much longer time to conduct any Design, for the Good of the Common-wealth, to its Maturity and Perfection.

definitions.definition: To publish in church for marriage; said of both the banns and the persons.
(figuratively) To take (a person's situation) as an example.

quote.citation: 1990 April 26, Paul Wiseman, “Dark days”, in USA Today:
quote.text: Even when the damage isn't that clear cut, the intangible burdens of a bad image can add up. Just ask Dow Chemical.

definitions.definition: An act or instance of asking.

quote.text: To ask for a gift is a privilege, a wonderful expression of commitment to and ownership of the organization. Getting a yes to an ask can be a rush, but asking for the gift can and should be just as rewarding.

quote.citation: 2022 December 14, Christian Wolmar, “No Marston Vale line trains... and no one in charge seems to 'give a damn'”, in RAIL, number 972, page 46:
quote.text: That really does not seem much of an ask.

quote.citation: 2008, Doug Fields, Duffy Robbins, Speaking to Teenagers:
quote.text: Communication researchers call this the foot-in-the-door syndrome. Essentially it's based on the observation that people who respond positively to a small “ask” are more likely to respond to a bigger “ask” later on.

definitions.definition: (Internet) A message sent to a blog on social networking platform Tumblr, which can be publicly posted and replied to by the recipient.

quote.citation: 2017, Abigail Oakley, “Supporting one another: Nonbinary community building on Tumblr”, in Isabel K. Düsterhöft, Paul G. Nixon, editors, Sex in the Digital Age, unnumbered page:
quote.text: Answering 'asks' like this is one common way that Tumblr bloggers interact with their followers, so it is in the act of publicly answering these asks that I examine community building practices.

quote.citation: 2018, Lynette Kvasny, Fay Cobb Payton, “African American Youth Tumbling Toward Mental Health Support-Seeking and Positive Academic Outcomes”, in Amanda Ochsner, William G. Tierney, Zoë B. Corwin, editors, Diversifying Digital Learning: Online Literacy and Educational Opportunity‎[1], page 168:
quote.text: The following example from Black Mental Health illustrates an ask from an anonymous follower seeking social support:  […]

quote.citation: 2020, Lee Brown, “Behind the Scenes of a Popular Trans Youth Resources Tumblr”, in Alexander Cho, Allison McCracken, Indira N. Hoch, Louisa Stein, editors, A Tumblr Book: Platforms and Cultures‎[2], page 265:
quote.text: Once the number of unanswered Asks in the inbox was over eight thousand, despite us deleting everything accumulated in the inbox once a year.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English aske, arske, ascre, from Old English āþexe (“lizard, newt”), from Proto-West Germanic *agiþahsijā (“lizard”), a compound of *agiz (“snake, lizard”) + *þahsuz (“badger”). Cognate of German Echse (“lizard”).

definitions.definition: (UK dialectal and Scotland) An eft; newt.

quote.text: He looked at the beast. It was not an eel. It was very like an ask.

quote.citation: 1951, Malcolm Arthur Smith, The British Amphibians & Reptiles, page 258:
quote.text: We hear of Adder dens, but detailed accounts of the discovery of one are very rare. Service (1902) records that a peatman, when levelling on an estate by the Solway, found in a hole in the ground, some 8 inches below the surface, 40 adders, 10 toads and a large number of asks (lizards).
